en: The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Linji Huizhao of Zhenzhou, Compiled by His Dharma Heir and Junior Disciple Huiran While Residing at Sansheng.
The Provincial Governor, Attendant Wang Changshi, together with various officials, requested the Master to ascend the seat. The Master entered the hall and said: "The mountain..."
Today, the Sangha has no choice but to comply with human sentiment and ascend this seat.
However, if we were to discuss the Great Matter according to the tradition of our ancestral masters, it would be truly impossible to open one's mouth; there would be no place for you to set foot.

Today, at the earnest request of the Attendant Jian, this mountain monk has brought forth the essential thread of the school’s lineage. Is there any master warrior here who can immediately unfurl his banner and deploy his array?
Let him come forward and provide proof before the assembly.
A monk asked,
"What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?
The Master gave a shout, and the monk bowed.
The Master said,
"This monk is indeed capable of engaging in debate.
He then questioned the Master:
"Whose song are you singing?
Whom do you succeed in the lineage of the school's wind?
The Master said:
“I asked Huangbo three times and was struck three times.
As the monk hesitated, the Master gave a shout, followed by a blow, saying:
“One must not try to drive a stake into empty space.”
A presiding abbot asked,
"Are not the teachings of the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the canon the very elucidation of Buddha-nature?
The Master replied:
"The wild grass has never been weeded.
The Master said,
"How could the Buddha deceive people?"
The Master said,
"Where is the Buddha?
The host was speechless.
The Master said, "If you intend to deceive this old monk in the presence of the Attendant-in-Ordinary, withdraw quickly, withdraw quickly! You are obstructing others from asking their questions.
He spoke again:
"This day’s Dharma assembly is for one great matter; is there anyone else who wishes to pose a question?
Come forward quickly with your inquiry! As soon as you open your mouth, you will already have missed the point."
Why is this so? Have you not seen that the World-Honored One Śākyamuni said:
"The Dharma is free from words and letters; it does not belong to causes, nor does it abide in conditions"?

"Because you do not have sufficient faith, I fear that today's entanglement will hinder the Attendant and the various officials, causing you to obscure your Buddha-nature; it would be better for you to withdraw for now."
He gave a shout and said:
"Those with little faith will never reach the end.
I have stood here for a long time; take care."
One day, the Master arrived at the Prefecture of He. The Prefectural Governor, Attendant Wang Changshi, invited the Master to ascend the seat.
At that time, Magu came forward and asked:
"The Great Compassionate One has a thousand hands and eyes; which one is the True Eye?"
The Master said:
"Of the thousand hands and eyes of Great Compassion, which one is the True Eye?
Speak quickly, speak quickly!"
Magu pulled the Master down from his seat; Magu then sat back down. The Master stepped forward and said, "How do you do?
As Magu hesitated, the Master likewise pulled Magu down from his seat; the Master then sat back down, and Magu immediately departed. The Master then descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, he said:

"Upon this ball of red flesh there is a true person of no rank who constantly enters and exits through the gate of the face of each and every one of you. Those of you who have not yet realized this—look, look!"
At that time, a monk came forward and asked,
"What is the true person of no station?
The Master descended from his meditation seat, seized him, and said:
"Way, way. As the monk hesitated, the Master pushed him away and said,
"What kind of dried-up dung pellet is the 'true person of no station'?"
He then returned to his quarters.
Upon ascending the hall, a monk came forward and prostrated; the Master immediately shouted.
The monk said:
“Old Monk, do not poke your head out!
The Master said,
“Tell me, where has it fallen?”
The Master then shouted.
Furthermore, another monk asked:
"What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?"
The Master then gave a shout; the monk prostrated, and the Master asked, "Tell me, was that a good shout?
The monk said:
"The grass bandits have been utterly defeated.
The Master asked,
"Where does the fault lie?"
The assembly said,
"A second offense will not be tolerated.
The Master then gave a shout.
On that day, the two head seats of the hall saw each other and simultaneously let out a shout.
A monk asked the Master,
"Is there still a distinction between guest and host?"
The Master said:
"Guest and host are clearly distinct.
The Master continued:
“If you great assembly wish to understand Linji’s phrases of host and guest, go and ask the two head seats in the hall.
He then descended from his seat.
Upon ascending the hall, a monk asked:
"What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?
The Master held up his whisk; the monk then shouted, and the Master struck him.
Again, a monk asked:
"What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?
The Master also held up his whisk. The monk then gave a shout, and the Master also shouted.
As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him.
The Master then said:
"O Great Assembly!
Now, those who take up the Dharma do not shrink from the loss of body or life."

For twenty years, I questioned the late Master Huangbo three times about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma; on each occasion, I received a blow from his staff, which felt as though it were merely being brushed by a stalk of mugwort.
"Now I am thinking even more of getting to eat a blow from the staff; who will act for me?
At that time, a monk stepped forward from the assembly and said, "I can do it."
The Master raised his staff and offered it to him; as the monk prepared to receive it, the Master struck him.
Later, while ascending the hall, a monk asked:
"What is the matter on the edge of the sword?"
The Master said, "A calamity! A calamity!
As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him.
Question:
"As for the practitioner in the stone chamber, while treading the pestle he forgot to move his foot; where did he go?
The Master said:
"He has drowned in a deep spring.
The Master then said, "To everyone who comes, I do not fail them; I recognize the place from which they come."
If you come in this way, it is as if you have lost [yourself];
if you do not come in this way, you bind yourself without a rope.
At all times, do not engage in confused deliberation; whether you understand or do not understand, it is all ultimately an error.
"Clearly stated thus, let everyone under heaven judge as they please.
Long standing; take care.
He ascended the hall and said:
"One person stands atop a solitary peak with no way to emerge;
another person stands at a crossroads with neither front nor back.
Which one comes first?"
Which one is behind?
He is neither Vimalakīrti nor Fu Dashi.
Take care.
Ascending the hall, he said:

"There is one person who remains on the road for kalpas without leaving home; there is another person who leaves home and is no longer on the road. Which of these two is worthy of receiving the offerings of devas and humans?"
He then descended from his seat.
Upon ascending the hall, a monk asked:
"What is the first phrase?"
The Master said:
"When the seal of the three essentials is opened, the vermilion dot is set askew; there is no room for deliberation, for host and guest are distinguished.
He asked:
"What is the second phrase?
The Master said:
"How could wondrous understanding fail to accommodate the question of Wuzhuo? How could the *upāya* (skillful means) fail to match the capacity to cut through the stream?"
Question: "What is the third phrase?
The Master said:
"Look at the puppets on the stage; their every movement is pulled by someone within.
The Master further said:
"A single phrase must embody the three mysteries (sanxuan), and each mystery must embody the three essentials (sanyao); there must be both skillful means (quan) and practical application (yong)."
"How do you all understand this?
He then descended from his seat.
Later that evening, the Master addressed the assembly in a formal discourse, saying:

"Sometimes the person is taken away but the environment is not; sometimes the environment is taken away but the person is not; sometimes both person and environment are taken away; and sometimes neither person nor environment is taken away."
At that time, a monk asked:
"What is 'taking away the person but not taking away the environment'?
The Master said:
"The warm sun brings forth life, spreading a carpet of brocade; the pearl-like infant’s hanging hair is white as silk.
The monk asked, "What is 'seizing the environment but not seizing the person'?"
The Master said:
"The Emperor’s decree has already been promulgated throughout the world; the generals beyond the frontier have cleared away all smoke and dust.
The monk said:
"What is meant by 'the human and the environment both being negated'?
The Master said:
"In Bing and Fen, all news is cut off; one dwells alone in a single place."
The monk asked,
"What is it like when both person and environment are not wrested away?
The Master said:
"When the King ascends the precious hall, the village elders sing songs of joy.
The Master then said:
"Those who study the Buddha-dharma today must first seek a genuine insight."
If you attain true and correct insight, you will be unstained by birth and death and possess freedom in going and staying; without seeking excellence, excellence will arrive of its own accord.
O followers of the Way!
As for the ancient masters of old, they all possessed a path for transcending the ordinary.
In the way I, this mountain monk, instruct people, I simply want you not to be deluded by others; when you need to act, act immediately, and do not hesitate for a moment longer.
Wherein lies the sickness of those students today who do not attain it?
It lies in their lack of self-confidence.
If you cannot have confidence in yourself, you will immediately become busily preoccupied with all external objects, being turned around by them; thus, you will not attain freedom.
If you can bring to rest this mind that incessantly pursues and seeks, you will be no different from the patriarchs and buddhas.
Do you wish to recognize the patriarchs and buddhas?
They are simply those who are listening to the Dharma right before you.
These practitioners lack sufficient faith and thus rush outward in pursuit.
Even if they manage to find something, it will all be merely the superior forms of words and texts; they will never attain the living ancestral meaning.

Do not err, O practitioners of Chan; if you do not encounter this at this very moment, you will wander through the three realms for ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes, chasing after pleasant appearances until they snatch you away, and you will be reborn within the bellies of donkeys and oxen.
"O followers of the Way!
According to my own perspective, I am no different from Śākyamuni.
In all the various applications of today, what is lacking?"
The divine light of the six realms has never ceased; if you can perceive it in this way, you will be a person of no concerns for the rest of your life.
Venerable sir!
The three realms offer no peace, like a house on fire; this is not a place where you may dwell for long.
The ghost of impermanence kills in a single kṣaṇa, making no distinction between noble and base, old and young.
You must be no different from the patriarchs and Buddhas; you simply must not seek outside.
The pure light within your single thought-moment is the Dharmakāya Buddha within your own house;
the non-discriminating light within your single thought-moment is the Sambhogakāya Buddha within your own house;
the undifferentiated light within your single thought-moment is the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha within your own house.

These three kinds of bodies are none other than the very people before you who are listening to the Dharma right now; it is precisely because they do not run outward in pursuit that this efficacy exists.

According to the masters of the sutras and śāstras, these three kinds of bodies are taken as the ultimate standard, but from the mountain monk’s perspective, this is not so: these three kinds of bodies are merely names and also the three kinds of supports.
The ancients said:
"The body is established based on its meaning; the land is discussed according to its substance.
Thus, it is clearly understood that the Dharma-nature body and the Dharma-nature land are but light and shadow.
"Virtuous One!
For now, recognize that the person who plays with light and shadow is the fundamental source of all Buddhas; every place is the dwelling where the lineage of the Way returns.

It is neither this physical body of the four elements that understands preaching or hearing the Dharma, nor the spleen, stomach, liver, and gallbladder that understand preaching or hearing the Dharma, nor empty space that understands preaching or hearing the Dharma. What, then, understands preaching and hearing the Dharma?"
This is that which is vividly present before your eyes—not a single form or segment, yet radiantly clear. This is what explains the Dharma and listens to the Dharma.
If you can see it in this way, then you are no different from the patriarchs and Buddhas.

However, at all times, do not allow this to be interrupted even for a moment; it is present before one's very eyes. It is only because emotions arise that wisdom is obstructed, and because conceptualizations shift that the essence becomes alienated; thus, one transmigrates through the three realms and undergoes manifold sufferings.
According to my own perspective as a mountain monk, there is nothing that is not profoundly deep and nothing that is not liberated.
O practitioners of the Way!

The dharma of the mind is formless and penetrates throughout the ten directions: when it is in the eye, it is called seeing; when it is in the ear, it is called hearing; when it is in the nose, it smells fragrances; when it is in the mouth, it engages in discourse; when it is in the hands, it grasps and holds; when it is in the feet, it moves and runs.
Originally there was one refined spirit, which divided into six harmonious combinations.
Once the single mind is absent, liberation occurs wherever one is.
When I, this mountain monk, speak in this manner, where does the meaning lie?
It is simply because you practitioners of the Way pursue everything with such intensity that your minds cannot find rest, and you fall into the idle conceptual realms of the ancients.

You practitioners of the Way should adopt my perspective: cut off the heads of the *nirmāṇakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya* Buddhas; even those whose minds are fulfilled in the ten stages are like hired laborers; those of the two levels of Equal Enlightenment and Wondrous Enlightenment are men bearing shackles and chains; Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas are like filth in a latrine; and Bodhi and Nirvana are like hitching posts for donkeys.
Why is this so? It is simply because you practitioners of the Way do not realize that the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* are empty; therefore, such obstacles arise.

If one is a truly authentic person of the Way, it will never be like this: they are merely able to dissolve past karma in accordance with conditions, putting on their clothes as circumstances dictate, walking when they wish to walk and sitting when they wish to sit, without a single thought of yearning for the fruit of Buddhahood.
Why is this so? An ancient said:
"If one wishes to perform deeds to seek Buddhahood, Buddhahood is the great omen of birth and death."
"Venerable Sir!

Time is precious; do not merely intend to dabble idly in learning Chan and studying the Way, identifying with names and phrases, or seeking out Buddhas, patriarchs, and spiritual friends—be careful that your intentions do not go astray."
"O practitioner of the Way!
You have only one father and mother; what more do you seek?
Reflect inwardly upon this yourself."
An ancient said:
"When Yantradatta lost his head, he sought the place where the mind ceases; therein lies no-matter.
O Virtuous One!

Furthermore, one must remain ordinary and not put on a pretense; there are certain ignorant, bald monks who immediately see gods and ghosts, pointing east and marking west, and predicting fine weather or rain.
Those of such a sort must all eventually pay their debts; there will come a day when they must swallow hot iron balls before the Old Lord Yama.
When the sons and daughters of good families are possessed by these kinds of wild fox spirits, they immediately begin to act strangely—blind, wretched creatures!
"The day for collecting the rice money is at hand.
The Master addressed the assembly, saying:
"Followers of the Way!..."
One must earnestly seek the true and correct insight to move freely throughout the world, so as not to be deluded by these various spirits and demons.
Being a person of noble status is a matter of no concern; simply do not engage in artificiality, but remain as you naturally are.
If you intend to go outside and seek it from others, looking for a foothold, you have erred.
You merely intend to seek the Buddha, yet "Buddha" is but a name and a phrase.
Do you recognize that which is rushing about in its quest?

The Buddhas and Patriarchs of the three periods and ten directions appeared solely for the sake of seeking the Dharma; those of the present day who study the Way do so solely for the sake of seeking the Dharma.
Only upon attaining the Dharma is the matter finished; as long as it has not been attained, one will continue to transmigrate through the five realms as before.
What is this Dharma?
This Dharma is the mind-dharma; the mind-dharma is formless, pervading the ten directions, and is manifest in use before one's eyes.

Because people’s faith does not reach it, they instead cling to names and phrases, seeking the meaning and measure of the Buddha-Dharma within words and letters—a discrepancy as vast as that between heaven and earth.
"Followers of the Way!
When this mountain monk preaches the Dharma, what Dharma does he preach?
He preaches the Dharma of the Mind-ground, by which one can enter the mundane and the sagely, the pure and the defiled, and the true and the conventional."

Furthermore, it is not you—whether true or conventional, ordinary or holy—who can bestow names upon all that is true or conventional, ordinary or holy; rather, the true, the conventional, the ordinary, and the holy cannot bestow names upon this person.
"Followers of the Way!
Seize it and use it immediately; do not attach names to it, for we call this the 'Mysterious Principle' (xuánzhǐ).

My preaching of the Dharma differs from that of others in the world. Suppose Manjusri and Samantabhadra were to appear before you, each manifesting their own form to inquire about the Dharma; as soon as they say, 'I ask the Master,' I have already discerned them."
I, this old monk, sit steadily; when other practitioners come to see me, I discern them all completely.
Why is this so? It is simply because my perspective is distinct:
externally, I do not grasp at ordinary beings or sages; internally, I do not dwell in the fundamental source. Having seen through to the bottom, I no longer harbor doubt or error.
The Master addressed the assembly, saying:
"Followers of the Way!

In the Buddha-dharma there is no place for the application of effort; it is simply the ordinary state of non-action—defecating, urinating, putting on clothes, eating food, and when weary, lying down to sleep..."
Fools laugh at me, but the wise alone understand.
As the ancients said:
"To apply effort directed outward is, in every case, the mark of a foolish and obstinate man."

"Therefore, wherever you may be, act as the master; wherever you stand, it is all true. Even when objects appear and change before you, they cannot be exchanged away. Even if you possess habitual tendencies from the past or have committed the five crimes of immediate retribution, these will themselves become the great ocean of liberation."

Nowadays, students of the Dharma do not recognize the teachings at all; they are like sheep that, when their noses are touched, immediately put whatever they encounter into their mouths. Failing to distinguish between master and servant, and unable to differentiate between guest and host, such as these enter the Way with a deviant mind. They cannot enter amidst the clamor of the world, yet they are called true renunciants—though they are in fact true householders.
Now, those who have left the household life must discern the ordinary, genuine understanding—discerning Buddha from Mara, the true from the false, and the ordinary person from the sage...
If one can discern in this manner, it is called true renunciation.

If one cannot distinguish between Mara and the Buddha, this is precisely leaving one household only to enter another; such a person is called a sentient being creating karma and cannot be termed a true renunciant.
Right now, there is one Buddha and Mara who are of the same substance and undifferentiated, like water and milk mixed together, which only the king of geese can distinguish by drinking the milk.
A practitioner of the Way with clear eyes strikes both Mara and Buddha alike.
"If you love the holy and hate the ordinary, you will float and sink within the sea of birth and death.
He asked, "What is the Buddha?"
"Regarding 'Māra,' the Master said:
'The place where your single thought of mind harbors doubt is Māra.'"

If you can realize that the myriad dharmas are unborn and that the mind is like an illusion or a transformation, such that not even a speck of dust or a single dharma remains, and everything is pure everywhere—this is the Buddha.

Yet, "Buddha" and "demon" are merely the two realms of defilement and purity. From the perspective of this mountain monk, there is no Buddha and no sentient beings; there is no past and no present. One who attains it simply attains it, without passing through time or seasons; there is no cultivation and no realization, no gain and no loss. At all times, there is no other dharma whatsoever.
"Even if there were a single dharma that surpassed this, I would say it is like a dream, like a magical illusion.
Everything I have spoken, O seeker of the Way,
is exactly so."

The one who is currently listening with solitary clarity and vivid presence before them is a person who is unimpeded everywhere, penetrating throughout the ten directions and exercising mastery over the three realms. Entering all objective conditions, they cannot be turned back by any distinctions; in a single kṣaṇa, they penetrate the Dharma-realm. Encountering a Buddha, they speak of the Buddha; encountering a Patriarch, they speak of the Patriarch; encountering an Arhat, they speak of the Arhat; encountering a hungry ghost, they speak of the hungry ghost. Wandering through lands in all places to teach and transform sentient beings, they never depart from a single thought-moment. Being pure wherever they are, their light permeates the ten directions, and the myriad dharmas are seen as one.
O followers of the Way!

It is only today that you, as great men, finally realize that fundamentally there is nothing to do. It is simply because you lack faith that you pursue and seek in every thought-moment, like cutting off your head to search for it again; thus, you cannot find rest.

For instance, when a Bodhisattva of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching enters the Dharma-realm and manifests his body, he still feels aversion toward the mundane world and aspiration for the Pure Land; such a person’s sense of selection and rejection has not yet forgotten the mind of defilement and purity.
According to the view of the Chan school, it is not like that either; it is simply that right now there is no further time or occasion.
Everything I say is merely a medicine applied to treat a specific ailment for a particular period; in total, there is no substantial dharma.
If you perceive it in this way, you have attained true renunciation; such a person can digest ten thousand taels of gold daily.
O practitioners of the Way!

Do not, in your haste, allow yourselves to be branded by teachers from all quarters who stamp their seals upon your faces, claiming, "I understand Chan, I understand the Way," with eloquence like a cascading torrent—these are all merely creating the karma for hell.
If one is a true seeker of the Way, one should not seek worldly excellence, but must urgently and earnestly seek genuine insight.
Only when one attains genuine insight and understanding becomes perfectly clear and luminous does one finally reach completion.
Question:
"What is true and authentic insight?
The Master said:

"You need only enter everywhere—the mundane and the sagely, the defiled and the pure, the lands of all Buddhas, Maitreya’s pavilion, and Vairocana’s Dharma-realm. In each place, you shall manifest the formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness of lands; the appearance of Buddhas in the world, their turning of the Great Wheel of Dharma, and their subsequent entry into Nirvana. Yet, you will see no signs of coming or going; though you seek their birth and death, they are utterly unattainable. Thus, you enter the Dharma-realm of non-arising and roam through lands everywhere, entering the Flower Treasury World."

One perceives that all phenomena are empty in nature; there are no real dharmas whatsoever, only the person who hears the Dharma without reliance. This is the mother of all Buddhas, for it is from non-reliance that the Buddha is born.
If one awakens to the absence of dependence, even Buddhahood is not attained.
To perceive attainment in this manner is the true and correct understanding.
Students who fail to realize this cling to names and phrases; they are thus obstructed by the labels of "ordinary" and "sage," which prevents their eye of the Way from becoming clear.

The twelve divisions of the teachings are all expressions intended to reveal the truth; yet students do not understand this, and instead generate interpretations based on the manifest names and phrases. Thus, they all rely upon and fall into the realm of cause and effect, failing to escape the cycle of birth and death within the three realms.
If you wish to attain freedom in the coming and going, the dwelling and departing, the liberation and attachment within birth and death, then right now recognize the one who hears the Dharma:
formless, signless, rootless, groundless, and without a place of abiding.

Vibrant and throbbing, it must involve myriad provisional arrangements; yet its point of application is precisely no-place. Therefore, the more one seeks to grasp it, the further away it becomes, and the more one strives for it, the more it eludes one; thus it is called "the secret."
"O practitioners of the Way! Do not cling to this dream-like, illusory companion; before long, you shall return to impermanence.

What thing do you seek within this world to call liberation? Seek only enough food to eat to sustain yourself through the passing time. Furthermore, you must seek out a true teacher; do not be negligent or pursue worldly pleasures."

Time is to be cherished, for every thought-moment is impermanent; on a coarse level, one is beset by earth, water, fire, and wind, while on a subtle level, one is pressed by the four characteristics of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing.
"O followers of the Way!
At this time, you must first recognize the four kinds of signless realms, so as not to be tossed about and struck down by them.
He asked:
"What are the four kinds of signless realms?
The Master said:
"The moment you harbor a doubt in your mind, you are obstructed by earth."
If your mind gives rise to a single thought of attachment, you will be drowned by water;
if your mind gives rise to a single thought of anger, you will be burned by fire;
if your mind gives rise to a single thought of joy, you will be blown away by wind.

If one can discern in this manner, one will not be turned by external objects, but will employ them at will: surging eastward and subsiding westward, surging southward and subsiding northward, surging from the center and subsiding at the periphery, or surging from the periphery and subsiding at the center; walking upon water as if on land, and walking upon land as if on water.
Why is this so? It is because one has realized that the four great elements are like dreams and illusions.
O follower of the Way!
That which hears the Dharma right now is not something that your four great elements can employ.
If you can perceive your four great elements in this way, then you will attain freedom in going and staying.
According to my own perspective as a mountain monk, do not disparage this teaching.
If you cherish the "sacred," then "sacred" is merely a name. There are certain students who seek Mañjuśrī on Mount Wutai; they have already made a mistake, for there is no Mañjuśrī on Mount Wutai.
Do you wish to recognize Mañjuśrī?
It is simply this functioning right before your eyes, which remains unchanged from beginning to end; when there is no doubt in any situation, this very thing is the living Mañjuśrī.
This single thought-moment of yours is the light of non-differentiation; everywhere it is entirely the true Samantabhadra.
This single thought-moment of yours can spontaneously untie its own bonds, attaining liberation wherever it goes—this is Avalokiteśvara.

The dharmas of samādhi function as both primary and secondary to one another; when they emerge, they emerge simultaneously—oneness is three, and three is oneness. Only by understanding it in this way can one truly begin to contemplate the teachings.
The Master addressed the assembly, saying:

"Those who study the Way today must first have self-confidence; do not seek it outwardly. Otherwise, you will all fall into idle sensory realms and fail to distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox."
It is simply that there being patriarchs and Buddhas are all matters within the traces of the teachings.

When someone brings up a single phrase—whether emerging from the hidden or the manifest—doubt immediately arises; it illuminates heaven and earth, yet when one seeks answers from others, one is left in great bewilderment.
A man of great character should not merely spend his days debating who is the master and who is the thief, arguing over right and wrong, discussing form and wealth, or engaging in idle talk.

In this mountain monastery, I make no distinction between monastics and laypeople; whenever anyone comes, I recognize them completely, regardless of where they may emerge. As for any sounds, names, or phrases they may utter, they are all but dreams and illusions.

Yet, one sees that the person riding upon the realm is the profound principle of all Buddhas; the Buddha-realm cannot itself claim, "I am the Buddha-realm. Rather, it is this man of no-dependence who emerges riding upon the realm.
If someone comes forth and asks me for the Buddha, I shall manifest from the realm of purity;
if someone asks me for the Bodhisattva, I shall manifest from the realm of compassion;
if someone asks me for Bodhi, I shall manifest from the realm of pure excellence.
When someone asks me about nirvana, I respond by emerging from the realm of quiescence.
While that realm comprises ten thousand varieties of differentiation, the person remains undifferentiated; therefore, I manifest forms in response to things, like the moon reflected in water.
O followers of the Way!
If you wish to attain that which accords with the Dharma, you must first be a true man of great capacity;
if you are weak and submissive, you shall not attain it.
Now, a cracked or chipped vessel—*xi* (upper tone) for the first character and *suo-jia* for the second—is unfit to hold clarified butter (*ghṛta*).

One who is like a great vessel simply must not allow themselves to be deluded by others; taking the initiative as the master wherever they are, they remain true in every situation, and no matter who comes before them, they do not accept anything.
If you harbor a single thought of doubt for even a moment, the Māra will enter your mind; just as when a Bodhisattva doubts, the Māra of birth and death finds an opportunity.
You need only cease such thoughts and seek nothing further outward; when objects arise, simply reflect upon them.
You need only believe in that which is being used right now; there is not a single thing.
A single thought-moment of yours gives rise to the three realms; following conditions and being affected by objects, it is divided into the six sense-fields.
What is lacking in your current practice?
In a single kṣaṇa, you may enter pure lands or impure realms, enter Maitreya’s pavilion, or enter the land of the Three Eyes; as you travel everywhere, you will see nothing but empty names.
Question:
"What is the land of the three eyes?
The Master said:
“I shall enter with you into the Pure and Wondrous Land, don the garment of purity, and teach the Dharma-body Buddha;
furthermore, I shall enter the Land of Non-differentiation, don the garment of non-differentiation, and teach the Reward-body Buddha;
furthermore, I shall enter the Land of Liberation, don the garment of radiance, and teach the Transformation-body Buddha.”

These three eyes and the lands they inhabit are all transformations based upon [the source]. According to the masters of the sutras and treatises, the Dharma-body is taken as the fundamental essence, while the Reward-body and Transformation-body are its functions.
From my own perspective, the Dharma-body does not understand how to preach the Dharma.
Therefore, the ancients said:
"The body is established based on its meaning; the land is discussed according to its substance.

It is clear that the Dharma-nature body and the Dharma-nature land are merely dharmas established for the sake of universal understanding. They are like an empty fist or yellow leaves used to deceive small children; what juice can one find upon thorns, awns, and withered bones?
Outside the mind there are no phenomena, and within it, nothing can be found;
what object is there to seek? Yet you all say:
"The Way has cultivation and realization."
"Do not err; even if there are those who cultivate and attain [realization], these are all merely the karma of birth and death.
You say that you practice the six perfections and the myriad deeds in unison, yet I see them all as the creation of karma."
To seek the Buddha and seek the Dharma is itself to create the karma of hell;
to seek a bodhisattva is likewise to create karma;
even to read the sutras and study the teachings is to create karma.
The Buddhas and the Patriarchs are people of non-action; therefore, whether conditioned and with outflows (*sāsrava*) or unconditioned and without outflows (*anāsrava*), they perform pure deeds.

There is a certain class of blind shavelings who, having eaten their fill, sit in meditation and practice contemplation, grasping at thoughts and leaks to prevent them from arising, and loathing clamor while seeking stillness—this is the dharma of external paths.
The Patriarch said:

"If you dwell the mind to observe stillness, lift the mind to reflect outwardly, withdraw the mind to clarify inwardly, or concentrate the mind to enter meditative absorption—all such practices are merely contrived efforts."
"If that is so, how can you who are listening to the Dharma in this manner now intend to cultivate it, realize it, or adorn it?
It is not something to be cultivated, nor is it something that can be adorned."
If you instruct others in adornment, all things will indeed be adorned; do not, however, err in this regard.
O practitioners!
Do not take these words from the mouths of such teachers as being the true Way or as the inconceivable teaching of a true spiritual friend.
"I am but an ordinary person; I do not dare to fathom that venerable elder. Blind fellow!
Your entire life you have held nothing but this kind of view, bringing shame upon these eyes of yours, shivering and chilled like a colt on a frozen ice field.
"I do not dare to disparage a good spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), for fear of committing verbal karma. O Dao-liu!

Only one who is a great good spiritual friend would dare to disparage the Buddhas and the Patriarchs, judge right and wrong throughout the world, reject the teachings of the Tripiṭaka, revile all the "little children," and seek out people amidst both adversity and favor. Therefore, for twelve years I have sought a single particle of karmic nature as small as a mustard seed, yet none could be found.
If one were like the "New-Bride Son" Chan Master, he would have been immediately terrified and driven out of the monastery, denied food, and left in a state of unease and misery.
Since ancient times, when the predecessors of old went everywhere and people did not believe them, it was only after they were successively expelled that their true worth was recognized.
If everyone everywhere were willing to accept you, what would you be capable of accomplishing?
Therefore, when the lion lets out a single roar, the jackals' brains split open.
O practitioners of the Way!
"In all other directions it is said that there is a path to be cultivated and a dharma to be realized.
What dharma do you say is to be realized?
What path do you say is to be cultivated?"
"What is it that you currently lack?
Where do you need repairs?

Later generations of young monks, failing to understand this, immediately place their trust in such wild fox spirits and enchantresses. These people claim to bind others by explaining matters, asserting that one must only attain Buddhahood through the correspondence of principle and practice and the preservation of the three karmas; such talk is like a fine spring drizzle.
An ancient said:
"When you encounter a person who has attained the Way on the road, do not, above all else, speak of the Way.
Therefore it is said:

If a person cultivates the Way but the Way does not manifest, ten thousand kinds of heterodox states will vie to arise. When the sword of wisdom emerges, not a single thing remains; before the light-side has appeared, the dark-side is already clear.
Therefore, the ancients said:
"The ordinary mind is the Way.
O Virtuous One!
What is there to seek?
Right now, before your very eyes, the person who listens to the Dharma without dependence is vividly and clearly manifest, never lacking anything.
If you wish to be no different from the patriarchs and Buddhas, simply see in this way; do not allow yourself to be misled by doubt.
When each thought is not different from the mind, it is called the living patriarch.
If the mind were different [from moment to moment], then essence and appearance would be distinct;
because the mind is not different, essence and appearance are not distinct.
Question:
"What is the state where mind and mind do not differ?
The Master said:
"What you intended to ask has already been resolved long ago; nature and characteristics are each distinct. You who follow the Way, do not err.
All phenomena, mundane and supramundane, lack self-nature and lack the nature of arising; they possess nothing but empty names, and these names themselves are empty."
To merely recognize these idle names as real is a great error.
Even if they exist, they are all objects of transformation based upon something else.
There is a basis for bodhi, a basis for nirvana, a basis for liberation, a basis for the three bodies, a basis for object and wisdom, a basis for bodhisattvas, and a basis for buddhas.
What were you looking for when you were just now searching within this transformed land?
Even the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings are all just used-up paper for wiping away impurities.
The Buddha is a phantom body, and the Patriarch is but an old bhikṣu; have you returned to your mother-given nature yet?
If you seek the Buddha, you will be seized by the demon of the Buddha;
if you seek the Patriarchs, you will be bound by the demon of the Patriarchs.
Since all seeking leads to suffering, it is better to remain without concern.
There is a certain class of shaven-headed bhikṣus who say to those studying the Way:
"The Buddha is ultimate; it was only after three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas of cultivation that his fruition was perfected and he finally attained the Way."
"O follower of the Way!
If you say that the Buddha is ultimate, for what reason did he lie down on his side and pass away between the twin śāla trees in the city of Kuśinagara eighty years later?"
"Where is the Buddha now?
You clearly know that he is no different from me in terms of birth and death.

You say that the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics constitute the Buddha; then a Wheel-Turning Sage King should also be a Tathāgata. It is clear, therefore, that these are but illusory transformations."
An ancient said:

"The Tathāgata displays the marks of his entire body merely to accord with worldly sentiments; fearing that people might give rise to the view of annihilation, he provisionally establishes empty names.
He speaks of the thirty-two and eighty marks as mere provisional words; this empty sound and apparent body are not the essence of awakening—formlessness is the true form."
"You say that the Buddha possesses the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and is thus inconceivable.
Yet all the devas, ṛṣis, asuras, and powerful spirits also possess supernormal powers; should they not also be Buddhas?"

Followers of the Way, do not err. It is just like when the asuras fought with Śakra, Lord of Devas; having been defeated, he led eighty-four thousand of his retinue into the hollow of a lotus fiber to hide.
"Is this not the holy one? What the mountain monk has cited are all instances of karmic supernormal powers (*karmarddhi*) and dependent supernormal powers (*āśrayarddhi*).

As for the six supernormal powers of a Buddha, it is not so: entering the realm of form, he is not deluded by form; entering the realm of sound, he is not deluded by sound; entering the realm of fragrance, he is not deluded by fragrance; entering the realm of taste, he is not deluded by taste; entering the realm of touch, he is not deluded by touch; entering the realm of phenomena, he is not deluded by phenomena. Thus, he realizes that these six—form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and phenomena—are all empty in nature and cannot bind him."
"This man who walks without reliance, though his physical substance consists of the five aggregates and outflows, possesses the spiritual powers that move upon the earth. O practitioner of the Way!
