Now, for one who truly studies the Way of the Buddhas, they do not grasp at Buddhas, nor grasp at Bodhisattvas or Arhats, nor grasp at the excellence of the triple world. They are utterly detached and alone, liberated and unconstrained by things; even if heaven and earth were overturned, they would have no further doubts. When the Buddhas of the ten directions appear before them, they feel not a single thought of joy; when the three miserable realms and the hells suddenly manifest, they feel not a single thought of fear.

Why is this so? I perceive that all dharmas have the characteristic of emptiness: they exist when transformed and do not exist when untransformed. The triple world is but mind; the myriad dharmas are but consciousness. Therefore, why labor to grasp at dreams, illusions, or flowers in the sky?

Only those in the lineage of the Way who are presently listening to the Dharma here before me—when entering fire are not burned, when entering water are not drowned, when entering the three miserable realms of hell they wander as if visiting a garden, and when entering the realms of hungry ghosts and animals they do not undergo retribution.
Why is this so? Because there is no dharma that can be disparaged.
If you love the holy and hate the common, you will sink and float within the sea of birth and death.
Afflictions exist because of the mind; if there is no mind, what can afflictions constrain?
Do not trouble yourself with conceptual discrimination or grasping at signs; you will naturally attain the Way in an instant.

If you intend to learn by following others through endless toil, you will ultimately remain within birth and death throughout three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas. It would be better to sit cross-legged without concern at the corner of a bed in a forest thicket.
“O followers of the Way!
When students come from various quarters and the host and guest have completed their mutual greeting, there is immediately a single phrase:

‘To test whether the prior good friend can be led by the student to produce a word of expedient means and fling it past the corners of the good friend’s mouth—to see whether you recognize it or not.’”
"If you can recognize this object and seize it, then cast it straight into the pit.
When the student then returned to his ordinary state, he subsequently sought the words of the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), who again seized him as before.
The student said, "He is of superior wisdom; he is a great spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra). He then said:
"You truly do not know how to distinguish between the good and the bad.

It is like a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) taking up a piece of bait and dangle it before a student; if the student can discern it, they will act as their own master in every instance and remain undeluded by external conditions.
The spiritual friend immediately manifested half his body, whereupon the student shouted.
The spiritual friend then entered into all paths of differentiated speech and maneuvered about him;
the student said, "I do not recognize you, you old shaven-headed slave who knows neither good nor evil!"
The spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) praised him, saying:
"Truly a follower of the Way!

Yet, when other spiritual friends in various regions fail to distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, and a student comes to inquire about bodhi, nirvāṇa, the three bodies (trikāya), and the realm of wisdom, these blind teachers proceed to explain them to him. When they are rebuked by that student, they take up their staffs and strike him, saying:
"This is a lack of propriety.
From this point on, you who are good spiritual friends must not be blind; you must not harbor anger toward others.

There is a certain class of ignorant, ill-behaved shavelings who point east and mark west—praising fine weather, praising rain, or praising the lanterns and pillars. Look at how many hairs are on your eyebrows! Those students who possess the karmic conditions for this teaching do not understand it, and their minds immediately go mad.

Such as these are all merely wild fox spirits, demons, and goblins; they are met with loud laughter by those who truly seek the Way, who say: "This blind, old, shaven-headed slave is deluding the people of the world!"
"O followers of the Way!
Those who have left the household life must first study the Way. For instance, in my own past days, I applied my mind to the Vinaya and also sought out and investigated the sutras and śāstras."
Only later did he realize that these were expedient teachings intended to manifest the medicine for saving the world; he then cast them all aside at once and went to seek the Way and study Zen.
Subsequently, upon meeting a great spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), his eye of the Way finally became clear, and he began to truly recognize the world.
The old monk knew what was heterodox and what was orthodox; this is not something one knows from birth, but rather comes through investigation, refinement, and a sudden realization on a single day.
"O seeker of the Way!..."

If you wish to attain a realization that accords with the Dharma, simply do not allow yourself to be deluded by others; whether encountering things internally or externally, kill them as soon as you meet them—kill the Buddha when you meet the Buddha, kill the Patriarchs when you meet the Patriarchs, kill the Arhats when you meet the Arhats, kill your parents when you meet your parents, and kill your kinsmen when you meet your kinsmen—and only then will you attain liberation.

Not constrained by external things, one attains liberation and sovereign freedom. Among the seekers of the Way from all quarters, there has never been one who emerged without relying on some object. Here at this mountain monastery, I strike from the very beginning:

when something emerges from the hand, I strike with the hand; when it emerges from the mouth, I strike with the mouth; when it emerges from the eye, I strike with the eye. Not a single person has emerged in solitary detachment; they have all merely fallen into the idle realms and conditions of the ancients.
I, this mountain monk, possess not a single dharma to give to others; I do nothing but treat illnesses and untie bonds.
You practitioners from all quarters, try to come forth without relying on external things, and I shall deliberate with you.

In ten years or five years, not a single person among them has appeared; they are all mere spirits dwelling in grass and leaves, or wild foxes and goblins haunting bamboo and wood. They recklessly gnaw at every lump of dung, wasting in vain the offerings of the faithful from the ten directions. Claiming, "I am a renunciant," they hold such views as these, saying to you:
"There is no Buddha, no Dharma, no cultivation, and no realization. What is there for you to seek by following such outsiders?
"A blind man placing a head upon his own head—what is it that you lack?
O practitioners!
That which you employ before your very eyes is no different from that of the Patriarchs and Buddhas; yet you simply do not believe this, and so you seek it elsewhere."
Do not err; there is no dharma outside, nor can it be found within.
Rather than grasping at the words from this mountain monk’s mouth, it would be better to simply rest and be free of affairs.
Do not continue what has already arisen; do not intentionally give rise to what has not yet arisen. This would be superior to ten years of traveling on pilgrimage.
From the perspective of this mountain monk, there are no such various matters; it is simply the ordinary matter of putting on clothes, eating food, and passing the time without affairs.
"All of you who have come from various directions possess the intention to seek the Buddha, seek the Dharma, seek liberation, and seek deliverance from the three realms.
You fools!
If you must leave the three realms, where will you go?"
The Buddhas and Patriarchs are merely names and phrases tied to appearances.
Do you wish to recognize the triple world?
It is not separate from the very mind-ground upon which you now listen to the Dharma.

A single thought-moment of greed is the realm of desire; a single thought-moment of anger is the realm of form; a single thought-moment of delusion is the formless realm—these are the pieces of furniture within your house.
The three realms do not say of themselves,
"I am the three realms.
It is likewise, O follower of the Way!
O Virtuous One! At present, you who clearly and brilliantly illuminate and discern all manner of worlds have bestowed names upon those within the three realms.

This physical body composed of the four great elements is impermanent; even down to the spleen, stomach, liver, gallbladder, hair, fur, nails, and teeth—therein one perceives only the empty nature of all phenomena.
The place where your single thought-moment comes to rest is called the Bodhi tree;
the place where your single thought-moment cannot come to rest is called the tree of ignorance.

Ignorance has no dwelling place; ignorance has no beginning or end. If you cannot bring your mind to rest moment by moment, you will climb the tree of ignorance and enter the six realms and four modes of birth, with fur and horns upon you.
If you can bring it to rest, this is the realm of the pure body.

When not a single thought arises, you have already ascended the Bodhi tree; the supernatural powers and transformations of the triple world are the transformation-body born of mental cultivation. With the joy of the Dharma and the bliss of dhyāna, the radiance of your own body illuminates itself; when you think of clothing, a thousand layers of fine silks appear, and when you think of food, a hundred flavors are fully provided, with no further afflictions or illnesses.
Enlightenment has no place of abiding; therefore, there is no one who attains it.
"O follower of the Way!
Great man, what more is there for you to doubt?"

As for its present application, whoever can grasp it may employ it at will; do not cling to names, for this is called the Mysterious Principle. If you can see it in this way, do not disparage such a teaching.
An ancient said:
"The mind turns with the myriad objects; where it turns, it can indeed be profound. If one recognizes one's nature while following the flow, there is neither joy nor sorrow.
O followers of the Way!

In the Chan school’s understanding of life and death, the process is as natural and constant as this: when a master and disciple meet, there is an exchange of words; sometimes he manifests his form in response to things, or functions with his whole being; sometimes he employs skillful means through expressions of joy or anger, or reveals only half his body; sometimes he rides a lion, or rides an elephant king. One who studies must be extremely careful and discerning regarding such matters.
Suppose there is a genuine student who, upon being addressed, immediately shouts and first produces a lacquer basin.
The teacher of good knowledge, failing to discern this as a trap, enters that realm and begins to affect various postures and gestures.
The student then shouts, but the former person refuses to let go.
This is a terminal illness beyond medical cure; it is called "the guest looking at the host.
Alternatively, if the spiritual teacher (Sanskrit: *kalyāṇamitra*) does not bring forth any object, he seizes [the student's position] immediately according to the point of the student's inquiry.
When a student is seized and will not let go even unto death, this is the host looking at the guest.

Or, there may be a student who presents a single pure object before a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra); if the spiritual friend can discern that object and seize it to cast it into a pit, [the student has succeeded].
The student said,
"A truly great spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
He then said:
"Alas! You do not recognize good from evil.
When the student then prostrates, this is called "the host looking at the host.

Or there may be a student who comes before the spiritual friend wearing a cangue and shackles; the spiritual friend further places another layer of cangue and shackles upon him, and the student rejoices.
When these two cannot be distinguished from one another, they are called "guests looking at guests.
"Virtuous One!
All that this mountain monk has thus raised is for the purpose of discerning demons and selecting the extraordinary, so as to know what is heterodox and what is correct."
"O followers of the Way!
True reality is profoundly difficult to grasp, and the Buddha-dharma is subtle and profound;

yet it can be understood to some degree. Though I, this mountain monk, spend the entire day breaking it down for you, the students pay no heed. Even after passing over it ten thousand times underfoot, it remains pitch black and void, yet it is vividly and singularly luminous."

When practitioners lack sufficient faith, they produce interpretations based merely on names and phrases; even when reaching middle age, they continue to carry the corpses of others for hire, wandering the world with their burdens upon their shoulders—the day will surely come when they must pay for their straw sandals.
"Virtuous One!
This mountain monk says there is no dharma outside.

When students do not understand this, they immediately form an interpretation within; they sit leaning against a wall with their tongues pressed against the upper palate, remaining in a state of profound stillness and motionlessness, taking this to be the Buddha-dharma of our ancestral school."
A great error! If you take this unmoving, pure state as being correct, you are identifying ignorance as your master.
As the ancients said:
"The profound abyss of dark stillness is truly terrifying."
"This is precisely it.
If you were to recognize that which moves as being 'it,' then all grasses and trees would understand movement, and they too should be the Way.
Therefore, that which moves is the element of wind, and that which does not move is the element of earth; both movement and non-movement are devoid of intrinsic nature."
If you try to seize him where he moves, he stands where he does not move;
if you try to seize him where he does not move, he stands where he moves.
For example, it is like a fish submerged in a spring that stirs the waves to leap forth.
Venerable Sir!
Motion and non-motion are two kinds of objects, yet both are without support; the practitioner of the Way employs both motion and non-motion.
When practitioners from various quarters come here, I, this mountain monk, apply three ways of severing their faculties:
if those of middling or inferior faculties come, I seize away their objective realm but do not remove their dharma;
if those of superior faculties come, I seize away both their objective realm and their dharma.
If someone of the highest capacity comes, I do not take away their realm, their person, or their Dharma;
if someone with extraordinary insight comes, I, this mountain monk, function here as the whole body without passing through the stages of the faculties.
"Virtuous One!
Arriving here, the place where this student exerts effort allows no passage for the wind; even a spark of stone or a flash of lightning has already passed by.
If the student’s eyes flicker, there is no connection; if one conceives a thought, it is already mistaken; if one stirs a single念 (nian), it is already deviant."
There are those who understand that it is not apart from what is before one's eyes.
Venerable sir!

As you carry your alms-bag and your "dung-basket" about, running from house to house seeking the Buddha and seeking the Dharma—do you recognize this very person who is currently thus rushing about in search?

Vibrant and lively, it is simply rootless; you cannot gather it by grasping, nor can you disperse it by pushing away. If you seek to cling to it, it recedes further; if you do not seek it, it is already present before your eyes.
The spiritual resonance reaches your ears; if you do not believe this, your hundred years of toil will be in vain.
"O follower of the Way!

In a single kṣaṇa, you enter the Flower Treasury World (Avataṃsaka-lokadhātu), enter the land of Vairocana, enter the land of liberation, enter the land of supernormal powers, enter the land of purity, enter the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), enter the defiled and the pure, enter the mundane and the sagely, and enter the realms of hungry ghosts and animals. Everywhere you search and seek, you find nothing that has birth or death—there is only an empty name."
Illusory transformations and empty flowers need not be grasped; let gain and loss, right and wrong, be cast off all at once.
"Followers of the Way!

This mountain monk’s authentic transmission of the Buddha-dharma has come down from Venerable Magu, Venerable Danxia, Venerable Daoyi, and Venerable Yuezhitou of Mount Lu. I have traveled this path throughout the world, yet no one believes it, and all have raised slander."
When Master Daoyi’s functioning was pure and without admixture, three hundred or five hundred students could not perceive his intent at all.
When Master Lushan functioned with sovereign authenticity, whether in accord or in opposition, the students could not fathom its limits and were all left in a state of bewilderment.
For instance, when Master Danxia played with his pearl, appearing and disappearing, all students who came were scolded by him.
When Magu applied his method, it was as bitter as yellow-barked galls; none could approach him.
Just as when Shigong applied himself, people were terrified by those who came seeking him on the tip of his arrow;

so too, the way this mountain monk applies himself today—truly accomplishing both creation and destruction, playing with divine transformations, entering all realms, remaining free from affairs wherever he goes—is such that external circumstances cannot alter him.

"Whenever anyone comes seeking me, I immediately go out to look at them; they do not recognize me, so I put on various kinds of clothes and imitate human beings to enter their realm of understanding, saying: 'Alas!
You blind shavelings, you sightless people, take the clothes I am wearing and identify them as blue, yellow, red, or white. Then I strip them off and enter the realm of purity."
As soon as the student saw this, he felt a sense of longing and desire.
When I took it off again, the student lost his composure; in a state of frantic agitation, he ran about, crying out, "I have no clothes!"
I immediately called out to him, saying,
"Do you recognize the person who is wearing these clothes?
He suddenly turned his head and recognized me.
"Virtuous One!

Do not claim this robe as yours; the robe cannot move of itself—it is the person who can wear it. There is the robe of purity, the robe of non-arising, the robe of bodhi, the robe of nirvana, the robe of the patriarchs, and the robe of the Buddhas."
"Venerable One!

All that exists as sound, name, and phrasing is merely a transformation of clothing; stirred up from the ocean of wind-energy at the navel-wheel and formed into their respective meanings by the clashing of teeth, they are clearly known to be illusory transformations."
"Virtuous One!
External vocal karma and internal mental factors (caitta-dharma) arise from volition (cetanā) and mindfulness (smṛti); all of these are but garments.

If you merely recognize the clothes worn by others as true understanding, then even after passing through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, you will only be permeated by garments, wandering through the three realms and cycling in birth and death."
"It would be better to do nothing at all—meeting without recognizing one another, speaking together without knowing each other’s names.

Nowadays, students fail to attain realization because they mistake names for understanding; they copy the words of dead old men onto large tablets, wrapping them in layers upon layers of commentary, not allowing others to see them, claiming these are profound mysteries and treating them as precious treasures."
A great error! You blind fellow!
What kind of juice are you seeking upon a withered bone?

There is a certain class of people who, failing to distinguish between good and evil, take the meaning from the teachings and engage in speculative deliberation to construct phrases and meanings; it is like taking a lump of excrement into one's mouth, spitting it out, and passing it on to another.
It is like an ordinary person who plays the game of "whispered commands"; their entire life passes in vain.

They claim to have left the household life, yet when questioned about the Buddha-dharma, they immediately fall silent and are at a loss for words; their eyes are as dull as pitch-black lacquer and their mouths are like wooden door-panels. Those of such a kind, even upon the appearance of Maitreya in the world, shall be transported to another world-system to dwell in hell and undergo suffering.
"Venerable sir!
Where have you been wandering to all these places looking for what?
Your soles are broad enough; there is no Buddha to be sought, no Way to be realized, and no Dharma to be attained."
"Seeking an external Buddha with form is not like you; if you wish to recognize your original mind, it is neither joined nor separate.
"O practitioner of the Way!

The true Buddha has no form, the true Way has no substance, and the true Dharma has no characteristics. These three dharmas are blended and unified into one place; since they cannot be distinguished, such people are called sentient beings of the frantic karmic consciousness."
Question: "What is the true Buddha?
What is the true Dharma?"
"What is the True Way?
I beg you to grant me instruction.
The Master said:
“The Buddha is the purity of mind;
the Dharma is the luminosity of mind;
and the Path is the pure radiance that is unimpeded everywhere.”
The three are identical with the one; all are merely empty names and lack substantial reality. This is like a true practitioner of the Way whose mind remains uninterrupted from moment to moment.
Since Master Bodhidharma came from the Western Land, he sought nothing other than a person who would not be deluded by others.
Later, upon meeting the Second Patriarch, he attained realization through a single word and finally understood that all his previous efforts had been in vain.
My own insight today is no different from that of the patriarchs and Buddhas: if one attains it within the first phrase, one becomes a teacher of the patriarchs and Buddhas;
if one attains it within the second phrase, one becomes a teacher of gods and humans.
"If you attain it within the third phrase, you will not even be able to save yourself.
He asked,
"What is the meaning of the Westward Journey?"
The Master said:
"If you have a deliberate intention, you will not even be able to save yourself.
He asked:
"If there was no intention, how did the Second Patriarch obtain the Dharma?
The Master said,
"To obtain it is to not obtain it."
[The student] asked:
"Since it cannot be attained, what is the meaning of this 'cannot be attained'?
The Master said:
"Because you have been running and seeking everywhere, your mind cannot find rest.
Therefore, the Patriarch said: 'Alas, O man!'"
"Seeking the head with the head.
If you can immediately reflect back upon yourself at these words, you will no longer seek elsewhere.
Knowing that body and mind are no different from the patriarchs and Buddhas, you will find yourself without affairs in this very moment; only then is it called "attaining the Dharma."
"Virtuous One!
At this time, I, the mountain monk, have no choice but to speak out of necessity, though it results in much impurity of expression.
Do not misunderstand me; according to my own realization, there are truly not so many varieties of principles. When needed, they are used; when not needed, they are simply set aside."

As for what is preached everywhere—that the six perfections and ten thousand practices constitute the Buddha-dharma—I say these are merely gates of adornment and gates of Buddha-activity, not the Buddha-dharma itself. Even those who observe fasts and precepts, or carry oil without spilling a drop, if their eye of the Way is not clear, they must all pay their debts; the day will come when they must pay the price of their food.
Why is this so? Because entering the Way without penetrating its principle, one returns to consume the offerings of the faithful.

Even if a householder is eighty-one years old, his trees will not grow; even if one dwells alone on a solitary peak, eats but one meal before noon, remains seated without lying down, and practices the Path during the six periods of the day—all such people are merely those who create karma. Even if one gives away everything—head, eyes, marrow, brain, kingdom, city, wife, children, elephants, horses, and the seven treasures—all such views are rooted in the suffering of body and mind, and thus they still invite bitter fruits. It is not as good as being free from affairs, pure and unadulterated.

Even Bodhisattvas at the stage of the fulfillment of the ten grounds cannot find any trace or footprint of this path upon seeking it; therefore, the various devas rejoice, the earth deities support his feet, and there are no Buddhas of the ten directions who do not offer praise.
Why is this so? It is because the practitioner who now listens to the Dharma leaves no trace in their activity.
He asked:
“The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū sat at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas, yet the Buddha-dharma did not manifest before him, and he could not attain the Way of Buddhahood.
I do not yet understand the meaning of this.”
"I beg the Master for instruction.
The Master said:
"Great Penetration (Dàtōng) is one's own self; to realize everywhere that all phenomena are without nature and without marks is called Great Penetration."
As for "superiority in wisdom," it means that in all places one has no doubts and does not apprehend even a single dharma; this is called superiority in wisdom.
As for a "Buddha," it is one whose mind is pure and whose radiance penetrates the entire Dharma-realm; thus he is named Buddha.
"Sitting at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas" refers to the ten pāramitās.
As for "the Buddha-dharma not appearing before one": since the Buddha is fundamentally unborn and the Dharma is fundamentally unextinguished, how could there be anything further to appear?
If one cannot attain the Way of Buddhahood, the Buddha would not have become a Buddha at all.
As an ancient said:
"The Buddha constantly dwells in the world, yet is not defiled by worldly dharmas."
"O follower of the Way!
If you wish to become a Buddha, do not follow after the myriad things.
When the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise; when the mind ceases, all manner of phenomena cease. When the one mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are without fault."
In both the mundane and supramundane realms, there is neither Buddha nor Dharma; they do not manifest before us, nor have they ever been lost.
Should anything appear to exist, it is all merely names and phrases, established as medicinal prescriptions for diseases to guide the immature, serving only to express names and sentences.

Furthermore, names and phrases do not name or phrase themselves; rather, it is that which is vividly manifest and spiritually alert right before you—the faculty of discernment, hearing, and knowing that illuminates all—that establishes all names and phrases.
"Venerable One!
Only by committing the five deeds of immediate retribution can one attain liberation.
He asked:
"What are the five deeds of immediate retribution?
The Master said:
"Killing one's father, harming one's mother, shedding the blood of a Buddha, causing a schism in the Sangha, and burning sutras and images—these are the five deeds of immediate retribution."
[The student] asked, "What is the father?
The Master said:

“Ignorance is the father. When you seek for a single moment of mind to find its place of arising and ceasing and cannot find it—like an echo in the void, with nothing to be found anywhere—it is called “killing the father.”
[The student] asked, "What is the mother?
The Master said:

"With craving as mother, if in a single thought-moment one enters the desire realm to seek that craving and perceives only the empty nature of all phenomena, being unattached in every place, this is called 'killing the mother.'"
[The questioner] asked:
"What is shedding the blood of the Buddha?
The Master said:
"If you do not give rise to even a single thought of conceptual understanding within the pure dharma-realm, you will be in darkness everywhere; this is shedding the blood of the Buddha.
He asked: "What is breaking the harmony of the Sangha?"
The Master said:

"When your single thought-moment is correctly directed toward the afflictions and fetters such that they are like space, having nothing upon which to rely, this is the breaking of the harmonious Sangha.
He asked:
"What is 'burning the sutras and images'?
The Master said:

"To see that causes and conditions are empty, the mind is empty, and dharmas are empty; to decisively sever [delusion] in a single thought, becoming utterly free from affairs—this is what it means to burn the sutras and images."
"Virtuous One!
If you attain realization in this manner, you will be free from being obstructed by the names of 'ordinary' or 'sage.

Yet, in a single thought-moment, you merely produce a false understanding based on an empty fist pointing at something; you falsely concoct strange notions within the phenomena of sense-bases and objects, becoming self-deprecating and disheartened, saying:"
"I am an ordinary person; he is a noble one.
Tulu! What such a desperate haste toward death?
Donning the skin of a lion, you yet let out the howl of a jackal. A man of great character does not fail to manifest the breath of a man;

yet you are unwilling to trust in that which belongs to your own house, seeking only outwardly. You merely follow the idle names and phrases of the ancients, relying on the shadows while seeking the light; you lack independent penetration. Encountering objects, you immediately become conditioned by them; encountering sensory dust, you immediately grasp at it. Delusion arises at every touch, and you have no standard of your own.
“O followers of the Way!
Do not grasp at the place where this mountain monk speaks. Why is that?
Such talk lacks any basis;
it is like attempting to paint the void for a period of time, as in the metaphors of painted images and the like.
O followers of the Way!
Do not take the Buddha as the ultimate; my view is that he is like a latrine hole.
Bodhisattvas and Arhats are all but shackles and fetters for binding people.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī wielded a sword to kill Gautama, and Aṅgulimāla took up a blade to harm the Śākyas.
O followers of the Way!

There is no Buddha to be attained; even the Three Vehicles, the Five Natures, and the traces of the Perfect and Sudden Teachings are all merely temporary remedies applied to specific ailments, and none possess any real, substantial dharma.
Even if such things exist, they are all merely similar in appearance—merely manifesting patterns and arranging characters; let us speak of it thus for now.
"O followers of the Way!
There is a certain class of shaven-headed ones who apply their efforts toward the internal, intending to seek the Dharma that transcends the world, but they have gone astray."
If a person seeks the Buddha, that person loses the Buddha;
if a person seeks the Way, that person loses the Way;
if a person seeks the Patriarch, that person loses the Patriarch.

"Venerable sir, do not err. For my part, I do not take your mastery of the sūtras and śāstras; nor do I take your status as a king or a great minister; nor do I take your eloquence that flows like a rushing river; nor do I take your cleverness and wisdom. I require only your genuine insight."
“O followers of the Way!
Even if you were to master a hundred volumes of sutras and treatises, it would not equal that of a single master who is free from affairs.

Your mastery—this leads you to despise others, to engage in the strife of victory and defeat, and to foster the ignorance of self and other, thereby increasing the karma for hell. It is like the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra, who, despite his mastery of the twelve divisions of the teaching, fell into hell in his very body, such that the great earth could not contain him.”
It is better to rest in non-action: when hungry, eat; when sleepy, close your eyes. Fools may laugh at me, but the wise alone understand.
O followers of the Way!

Do not seek within words; the movement of the mind leads to exhaustion, and inhaling cool air is of no benefit. It is better to realize in a single thought that dependent origination is birthless, thereby surpassing the provisional teachings of the three vehicles and the bodhisattvas.
"Virtuous One!
Do not let the days pass by in negligence.

In the past, when this mountain monk had not yet attained insight, everything was a dark, vast expanse; I could not let my time go to waste, and with a burning belly and an anxious heart, I hurried about seeking the Way. Only after gaining strength did I reach this day, where we can thus converse together as fellow seekers of the Way."

I exhort all practitioners of the Way not to labor for the sake of food and clothing; the world is easily passed through, but a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) is difficult to encounter, appearing only once in a great while like the udumbara flower.

"You all have heard from various quarters that there is an old fellow Linji who has appeared; you intended to pose difficult questions to him, but he left you speechless, as I have now manifested my entire being in action."
This student opened his eyes in vain; though his mouth moved, he was unable to utter a word, remaining dazed and ignorant as to how to answer me.
I said to him: "The trampling of dragons and elephants is not something a donkey can endure."

"In all those places, they merely pointed to their chests and tapped their ribs, claiming, 'I understand Chan; I understand the Way. Yet when three or two of them arrive here, they are at their wits' end. Alas!

You take this body and mind and wander everywhere, flapping two pieces of skin to deceive the common folk; the day will come when you shall eat iron rods. You are not sons of the renunciant life; you are all categorized within the realm of the asuras."

"Now, as for the Way of ultimate truth, it does not seek to stimulate or exalt itself through contentious debate, nor does it rely on resonant sounds to crush those of external paths; as for the successive transmission from Buddha to Patriarch, there is no other meaning beyond this."

Should there be verbal teachings, they fall within the scope of the transformative ritual of the Three Vehicles, the Five Natures, and the causes and effects of humans and devas; yet even such teachings as those of the Perfect and Sudden Vehicle are not otherwise [than this], for neither the youth Sudhana nor others seek any fault therein.
"Venerable sir!

Do not misapply your mind. Just as the great ocean does not harbor corpses, you are merely carrying this burden about as if to travel across the world; you have yourself given rise to the obstruction of views, which hinders your mind."
The sun rises without clouds, its beauty illuminating the heavens everywhere; there are no obstructions in the eye, nor flowers in the sky. O practitioner of the Way!

If you wish to attain accordance with the Dharma, simply do not give rise to doubt. When extended, it encompasses the entire Dharma-realm; when withdrawn, not even a thread or a hair is established. This vivid, solitary luminosity has never been lacking.
The eye does not see it, and the ear does not hear it; what thing would you call it?
An ancient said:
"To describe it as a single thing is to miss the mark."
"Just look for yourself; what more is there?
Though one could speak of it endlessly, each must exert effort for themselves.
Take care."
"Examine, examine! While Huangbo was entering the kitchen, he asked the rice steward, "What are you doing?
The rice steward replied:
"Selecting rice for the community of monks," Huangbo said,
"How much do you eat in one day?"
The rice steward said,
"Two shi and five [pecks].
Huangbo said:
"Is it not too much?
The rice steward replied,
"I am still afraid it is too little."
Huangbo then struck him.
The head cook reported this to the Master, who said,
"I shall test this old fellow for you."
As soon as he reached his place in attendance, Huangbo brought up the previous conversation, and the Master said, "The head cook did not understand;
please, Reverend, provide a turning word on his behalf."
The Master then asked,
"Is this not too much?
Huangbo said:
"Why do you not say, 'Come back tomorrow for another meal'?
The Master said,
"What is there to talk about tomorrow?"
"I will eat it right now.
Having said this, he struck him with his palm.
Huangbo said:
"This madman has come here again to stroke the tiger's whiskers.
The Master then shouted and sent him out.
Later, Guishan asked Yangshan:
"What was the intention behind these two venerable elders?
Yangshan asked. Yunyan said, "What about you, Master?"
Tiaoshan said,
"Only by raising children does one come to know a father's compassion.
Yangshan said:
"Not so," said Guishan. "And what about you?"
Yangshan said,
"It is very much like inviting a thief to ruin one's house.
The Master then asked a monk:
“Where have you come from?
The monk then gave a shout; the Master then bowed and invited him to sit.
As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him.
When the Master saw a monk approach, he raised his whisk; the monk bowed, and the Master struck him.
On another occasion, seeing a monk approach, he likewise raised his whisk; the monk paid no heed, and the Master struck him as well.
One day, while the Master was attending a vegetarian feast at a donor’s house together with Puhua, he asked:
"The hair of a tortoise swallowing the vast ocean, and a mustard seed containing Mount Sumeru— is this the wondrous function of spiritual powers?"
"What is the fundamental substance like?
Puhua kicked over the rice table.
The Master said:
"Too coarse," said Puhua.
"What kind of place is this to speak of coarse or fine?"
The next day, the Master again went with Puhua to a vegetarian feast.
He asked,
"How does today's offering compare to yesterday's?"
Puhua, as before, kicked over the rice table.
The Master said,
"You have succeeded, indeed, but you were far too crude."
Puhua said, "Blind fellow!
What 'coarse' or 'subtle' does the Buddha-dharma speak of?"
The Master then stuck out his tongue.
One day, while sitting with the Elder Mudata of Heyang inside the hearth of the Sangha Hall, the Master said:
"Puhua goes every day through the streets and markets acting like a madman; do you know whether he is an ordinary person or not?"
"Is this a sage?
Before he had even finished speaking, Puhua entered.
The Master then asked:
"Are you an ordinary person or a sage?
Puhua replied:
"Tell me, for a moment, am I a common person or a sage?
The Master then gave a shout.
Puhua pointed his finger and said:
"The bridegroom’s son from Heyang, the old woman’s Chan of the wooden pagoda, and the little page Linji—these three alone possess a single eye."
The Master said,
"This thief. Puhua said:
"Thief! Thief!
he cried, and then went out.
One day, Puhua was eating raw vegetables in front of the Sangha Hall.
The Master saw him and said,
"He looks very much like a donkey.
Puhua then immediately brayed like a donkey.
The Master said,
"This thief. Puhua said:
"Thief! Thief!
he cried, and then departed.
Thereafter, Puhua would constantly ring his bell in the marketplace, saying:

"If it comes from the bright side, strike it on the bright side; if it comes from the dark side, strike it on the dark side. If it comes from the four directions and eight corners, strike it with a whirlwind; if it comes from empty space, strike it by reaching up to the framework."
The Master sent an attendant away; as soon as he saw him approach in this manner, he seized him and said, "What if one does not come in this way at all?
Puhua pushed him away and said:
"Tomorrow there will be a vegetarian feast at the Great Compassion Temple," the attendant returned and reported this to the Master.
The Master said:
"I have always harbored doubts about this fellow.
An elderly master came to visit the Teacher; before even exchanging formal greetings, he asked:
"Is prostration the way?"
"Is not failing to prostrate the very point?
The Master then gave a shout; the elder monk then prostrated.
The Master said:
"What a fine grass-thief!
The old master said, "Thief! Thief!"
He then went out.
The Master said,
"Do not say that 'no affair' is good."
As the head seat stood in attendance, the Master asked,
"Is there still any transgression?
The head seat replied:
"Yes. The Master said,
"Has the guest committed an offense?"
"Does the host of the house have a fault?
The Head Seat replied,
"Both have faults."
The Master asked,
"Where does the fault lie?
The Head Seat then went out.
The Master said,
"Do not say that it is good to have nothing to do.
Later, a monk brought this up to Nanquan.
Nanquan said,
"Official horses trampling one another.
Because the Master was entering a military camp for a meal, he saw an officer at the gate and pointed to a pillar, asking:
“Is this an ordinary person?
Is this a sage?
The assembly remained silent and had no words to say.
The Master struck the pillar and said,
"Even if you could speak, you would still be nothing more than a wooden stake.
He then went inside.
The Master asked the head of the monastery,
"Where have you come from?
The head replied:
"The whole province is selling yellow millet.
The Master said,
"Have you sold it all?"
The host replied,
“I have sold it all.
The Master drew a line before him with his staff and said:
"Can you still sell this?
The host then shouted; the Master struck him.
When the steward arrived, the Master recounted the preceding words.
The head cook said,
"The abbot does not understand the Master's meaning.
The Master said:
"What do you say to this?
The head cook then prostrated, and the Master struck him as well.
Later, when a presiding lecturer came to pay his respects, the Master asked the lecturer:
"What sutra or treatise do you lecture on?
The host replied, "I am a person of shallow learning and coarse practice; I have studied the *Śata-dharma-śāstra*."
The Master said:

"Suppose there is one person who has clearly understood the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings, and another person who has not clearly understood the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings—are these two the same?"
"Are they different?
The Master replied, "If you understand, they are the same; if you do not understand, they are different."
Leyu was serving as the attendant and stood behind his master, saying:
"Master, what place is this? Are you speaking of sameness?"
"Speak something different!
The Master turned his head and asked his attendant:
"And what do you say?"
The attendant then gave a shout.
As the Master was escorting the abbot back, he turned to ask the attendant,
"Was it you who just now shouted at the old monk?"
The attendant replied,
“Yes. The Master then struck him.
When the Master heard that the second-generation Deshan was about to give this teaching,
saying, "Thirty blows for those who can speak it; thirty blows for those who cannot," he sent Le Pu to go and inquire.
"If you can explain it, why do you still receive thirty blows?
Wait until he strikes you; catch his staff and give it a shove to see what he will do.
When Wuxue arrived there, he questioned him exactly as instructed. Deshan struck him immediately; Wuxue caught the staff and gave it a shove, whereupon Deshan returned directly to his quarters.
Puhui brought this up for the Master to see, and the Master said, "I have always suspected this fellow; nevertheless, do you still see Deshan?"
As Puyi was about to offer a comment, the Master struck him.
One day, Wang Changshi visited the Master and, while looking together with him in front of the Sangha Hall, asked:
"Do the monks in this hall study the sutras?"
The Master said,
"I do not read scriptures.
The attendant asked:
"Do you still practice Chan?
The Master replied,
"I do not practice Chan."
The attendant said,
“If you neither study the sutras nor practice Chan, what exactly are you doing?
The Master said:
"I am generally instructing him to become a Buddha and an Ancestor.
The attendant asked, "Though gold dust is precious, if it falls into the eye, it becomes a cataract; what then?"
The Master said,
"I thought you were just an ordinary fellow.
The Master then asked Xingshan:
"What is the white ox on the open ground?
The Mountain said, "Hūṃ, hūṃ."
The Master said, "Dumb! Shan said:
"Venerable sir, what do you say?
The Master said, "This beast."
The Master asked Le Pu, "From the beginning until now, one person has practiced the staff and another has practiced the shout;
which of these two is more intimate? Pu replied:
“Not intimate at all.
The Master asked,
“What is the place of intimacy?”
The Master shouted at him, and the monk struck back.
Seeing the monk approach, the Master spread his two hands wide; the monk remained speechless, and the Master asked, "Do you understand?"
[The monk] said,
"I do not understand.
The Master said:
"The whole lump cannot be split open; I give you two copper coins.
When Dajue arrived for his formal interview, the Master raised his whisk, and Dajue spread out his sitting mat.
The Master threw down his whisk, and Da-jue gathered up his sitting mat and entered the Sangha hall.
The assembly of monks said,
"Is this monk perhaps a personal acquaintance of the Master?"
"He did not prostrate, nor did he accept the staff.
Upon hearing this, the Master ordered Jue to be summoned. When Jue came out, the Master said, "The assembly says that you have not yet had an audience with the Elder."
Jue said, “I do not understand,” and then returned to the assembly.
While Zhaozhou was traveling on pilgrimage, he visited a master. Upon encountering the master while he was washing his feet, Zhaozhou asked:
"What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The master said:
"It happens that this old monk is washing his feet.
The official stepped forward and made a gesture as if listening;
the Master said, "I shall give you another ladle of foul water to splash upon you."
The Governor then descended from his seat.
At that moment, the Venerable Ding arrived for an audience and asked,
"What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?"
The Master descended from his rope-couch, seized him, gave him a slap, and then pushed him away so that he stood there motionless.
A monk standing nearby said,
"Why does Master Ding not prostrate?"
Dingfang prostrated himself and suddenly attained great enlightenment.
When Magu arrived for an audience, he spread out his sitting mat and asked:
"Regarding the Twelve-Faced Avalokiteśvara, which face is the correct one?"
The Master descended from his rope-couch; with one hand he gathered up his sitting mat, and with the other he seized Magu, saying, "Where has the Twelve-Faced Avalokiteśvara gone?"
Magu turned around and prepared to sit upon the rope bed; the Master raised his staff and struck him. Magu caught the staff, and they grappled with one another as they entered the abbot’s quarters.

The Master asked a monk, "At times a shout is like the Vajra King’s precious sword; at times a shout is like a golden-maned lion crouching on the ground; at times a shout is like a probe or a blade of grass; at times a shout is not used as a shout. How do you understand this?"
The assembly hesitated, and the Master gave a shout.
The Master then asked a nun, "Welcome?"
"Come as an evil one?
Ni then shouted; the Master raised his staff and said, "Speak more, speak more!"
The nun shouted again, and the Master struck her.
Longya asked,
"What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?"
The Master said, "Bring me the meditation board.
Ya then passed the meditation board to the Master; the Master took it and struck him.
Ya said, "If you wish to strike me, go ahead and strike; however, it still lacks the meaning of the Patriarch.
Later, Ya went to Cuiwei and asked:
"What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Wei said,
"Hand me the meditation cushion."
Yaya then passed the meditation cushion to Cuiwei; Cuiwei took it and struck him.
Yaya said, "Strike as you will, but there is simply no meaning of the Patriarch in this."

Later, while Ya was staying at the monastery, a monk entered his room to seek instruction, saying, "When you were traveling on pilgrimage, you studied with two venerable elders; did you find their teachings acceptable?"
Ya said, "If you are willing, I am deeply willing; however, there is still no meaning of the Patriarch.
At Mount Jing, there was a congregation of five hundred people, yet few came to seek instruction. Huangbo sent the Master to Mount Jing and said to him:
"When you arrive there, what will you do?
The Master said,
"Upon arriving there, I shall have my own expedient means."
When the Master arrived at Jingshan, he girded his waist and ascended the Dharma Hall to see Jingshan.
Just as Jingshan raised his head, the Master let out a shout.
As Jingshan was about to open his mouth, the Master brushed his sleeves and departed.
Shortly thereafter, a monk asked Jingshan,
"What words did this monk just say that he shouted at you,
Master? Jingshan said:
"This monk has come from Huangbo’s assembly; do you wish to know?
Ask him first.
Thereupon, more than half of the five hundred followers at Jingshan dispersed.
One day, Puhua went among the people in the marketplace to beg for a *zhiduo* (a formal monastic robe). Everyone gave him one, yet Puhua would not accept any of them.
The Master ordered the monastery steward to purchase a coffin.
When Puhua returned, the Master said, "I have now made a *zhiduo* for you."
Puhua then carried it off himself, walking through the streets and markets while shouting:
"Linji has finished making a robe for me; I am going to the East Gate to pass away."
The people of the market vied with one another to follow and watch him.
Puhua said, "I have not finished today; tomorrow I shall depart for transformation at the South Gate."

Thus it was for three days; no one believed him, and on the fourth day, with no one following to watch, he went alone outside the city, entered the coffin himself, and requested a passerby to nail it shut. Immediately, news spread, and the people of the market vied with one another to go and open the coffin. They saw that his entire body had vanished, hearing only the faint sound of bells echoing away into the sky as he departed.
Regarding the *Xinglu*: When the Master was first in Huangbo’s assembly, his practice was pure and singular;
the Head Seat then sighed and said, "Though he is but a junior, he is different from the rest."
He then asked,
"How long have you been here, Senior?
The Master replied:
"Three years.
The Head Seat asked,
"Did Zeng Shen ever ask?"
The Master said, "You have never engaged in inquiry; you do not know what to ask.
The Head Seat replied:
"Why do you not go and ask the Abbot, 'What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?
The Master then went to ask; before he had even finished speaking, Huangbo struck him.
As the Master descended, the Head Seat said,
"What is the meaning of your question?
The Master replied:
Before [the monk] had finished asking his question, the Abbot struck him, and the monk said, "I do not understand.
The Head Seat said,
"Just go and ask again."
The Master went to ask again, and Huangbo struck him once more.
Thus he asked three times and was struck three times.
The Master returned and said to the Head Seat:

"By your great compassion, you have permitted me to inquire after the Master's health; yet though I asked three times, I was struck three times. I regret that my karmic obstacles prevent me from grasping the profound meaning, and so I shall now take my leave."
The Head Seat said, "If you are to go, you must take leave of the Abbot before departing.
The Master bowed and withdrew; the Head Seat then went first to the Abbot’s quarters and said:

"This young man who asks questions is truly in accord with the Dharma. If he comes to take his leave, you should skillfully receive him; in the future, he will grow into a great tree that will provide shade for all people under heaven."
The Master departed to take his leave of Huangbo, who said:
"You must not go elsewhere; you should go to Dayu at Tancheng in Gaoyang. He will surely explain it for you."
The Master went to Dayu, who asked,
"Where have you come from?
The Master said:
“[I] came from Huangbo.
Dayu asked, “What words did Huangbo say?”
The student said,
"I asked about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma three times and was struck three times.
I do not know if I have committed an offense."
"Are there no faults?
Daoyu said, "Huangbo has been so painstakingly compassionate for your sake that he has exhausted himself; yet you come here again to ask whether there are faults or not."
Upon these words, the Master attained great enlightenment and said,
"So it was that Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma was not much at all.
Dayu grabbed him and held him fast, saying:
“You bed-wetting brat! Just now you were saying whether there was an offense or not, and now you say that Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma is not much.
What principle have you seen?”
"Quick way! Quick way!
The Master struck Daoyu three times under the ribs; Daoyu pushed him away and said, "Your teacher is Huangbo; it is none of my business."
The Master took his leave of Dayu and returned to Huangbo.
Upon seeing him arrive, Huangbo immediately asked, "This fellow comes and goes; when will he ever reach a conclusion?"
The Master said,
"It is simply because my heart as an old woman is so earnest.
Having thus concluded the formal greetings, [the attendant] stood in attendance.
Huangbo asked,
"Where have you come from?
The Master replied:
"Yesterday, I received your compassionate command to go consult Dayu regarding his past and present.
Huangbo said,
"What words did Dayu have?"
The Master then recounted the previous conversation, and Huangbo said,
"How could I have let this fellow come here?
I would have given him a severe beating."
The Master said,
"What do you mean by 'waiting for it to come'?
Eat right now."
Thereupon he slapped him.
Huangbo said,
"This madman has come here to pull at a tiger's whiskers."
The Master then gave a shout.
Huangbo said,
"Attendant, lead this madman to the meditation hall."
Later, Guishan raised this story and asked Yangshan,
"At that time, did Linji receive the power of Dayu,
or did he receive the power of Huangbo?"
Yangshan said,
"Not only does he ride the tiger's head, he also knows how to grasp the tiger's tail.
While the Master was planting pine trees, Huangbo asked him:
"What is the purpose of planting so many [trees] deep within the mountains?
The Master replied, "First, to provide the mountain gate with a scenic setting; second, to serve as a landmark for future generations."
When he had finished speaking, he struck the ground three times with his hoe.
Huangbo said, "Even so,
you have already received thirty blows from me."
The Master again struck the ground three times with his mattock and made a sighing sound.
Huangbo said,
"Our school will flourish greatly in the world through you."
Later, Guishan raised this remark and asked Yangshan, “At that time, Huangbo entrusted his instructions to Linji alone; was there anyone else?
Yangshan replied:
“There was one, but because the time has been so long distant, I do not wish to cite him for you, Master.
Guishan said, “Even so, I still wish to know; you simply go ahead and cite him.”
Yangshan said, "One person pointed south toward Wu and Yue, where his commands were carried out; when he encountered a great wind, he stopped—this was a prophecy concerning Venerable Fengxue.
Later, while the Master was attending Deshan, Deshan said:
"Today I am exhausted.
The Master said,
"Why does this old fellow talk in his sleep?"
Baizhang struck him, whereupon the Master overturned the rope bed, and Baizhang then desisted.
Later, while the Master was working with the community to hoe the earth, he saw Huangbo approaching and stood leaning on his hoe.
Huangbo asked,
"Is this fellow tired?
The Master replied:
"Before the pickaxe has even been raised, what is there to be exhausted?
Huangbo then struck him. The Master caught the staff and gave it a shove, sending Huangbo tumbling over.
Huangbo called out:
“Karmadāna! Karmadāna!
Help me up!”
The rector stepped forward to support him, saying, "How can you, Reverend, tolerate such an impertinent, wind-crazed fellow?
As soon as Huangbo rose, he struck the rector; the Master then struck the ground with his hoe, saying:
"Everywhere else they perform cremation, but here we bury them alive all at once.
Later, Guishan asked Yangshan,
"What was the meaning behind Huangbo’s striking the rector?"
Yangshan said, "The real thief has run away; the one tracking his footprints is struck with a staff.
One day, as the Master was sitting in front of the Sangha Hall, he saw Huangbo approaching and immediately closed his eyes.
Huangbo then made a gesture of fear and returned to his quarters.
The Master followed him to the quarters to pay his respects and offer thanks; the Head Seat was standing in attendance there by Huangbo’s side.
Huangbo said:
"Although this monk is but a junior, he nonetheless knows that such a thing exists.
The Head Seat said,
"The Old Monk’s feet do not touch the ground, yet he provides testimony for a junior."
Huangbo slapped himself on the mouth. The Head Seat said, "If you know this, you have attained it.
While the Master was sleeping in the hall, Huangbo came down, saw him, and struck the head of the meditation platform once with his staff.
The Master raised his head and seeing it was Huangbo, went back to sleep.
Huangbo struck the wooden board once more, then went up to the upper section;
seeing the Head Seat meditating, he said, "The junior monks in the lower section are meditating, yet what are you doing here, indulging in such discursive thoughts?"
The Head Seat said,
"What is this old fellow doing?
Huangbo struck the wooden board once and then went out.
Later, Guishan asked Yangshan,
"What was Huangbo's intention in entering the Sangha hall?
Yangshan said:
"Two prizes for one wager.
One day, during a communal work assignment, the Master was walking behind. Huangbo turned his head and, seeing that the Master was empty-handed, asked:
"Where is the hoe?"
The Master said,
"There is one person who has already taken it away.
Huangbo said:
"Come closer; let us deliberate on a certain matter together.
The Master stepped forward, whereupon Huangbo held up his hoe and said, "This very thing—no one in the world can lift it up."
The Master reached out his hand, seized it,
and held it upright, saying, "Why is it now in my hand? Huangbo said:
"Today there is a great communal labor service," he said,
and then returned to the monastery.
Later, Guishan asked Yangshan:
"The pickaxe was in Huangbo’s hand; why, then, was it seized by Linji?
Yangshan replied, "The thief is a petty person, yet his cunning surpasses that of a gentleman."
The Master sent a letter to Mount Miao from Huangbo’s place; at that time, Yangshan was serving as the guest prefect, and upon receiving the letter, he asked:
"Is this for Huangbo?"
"Who is the special messenger?
The Master then struck him. Yangshan held him back, saying, "Brother, since you understand such matters, let it be."
They went together to see Guishan, who immediately asked,
"Brother Huangbo, how many followers do you have?
The Master replied:
"A gathering of seven hundred.
Miaoshan said, "Who acts as the leader?"
The Master said,
"I have already delivered the letter just now.
The Master then asked Moshan:
"Preceptor, how many people are in this assembly here?
Guishan replied,
"One thousand five hundred."
The Master said,
"Too much life. Guishan said:
“Brother Huangbo is no less so.
When the Master took his leave of Guishan, Yangshan saw him out and said,
“In the future, you will have a dwelling place to the north.”
The Master said,
"How could such a thing be possible?
Yangshan said:
"Simply go.
Hereafter there will be one person to assist my elder brother; this person has only a head but no tail, a beginning but no end.
Later, when the Master went to Zhenzhou, Puhua was already there.
When the Master appeared in the world, Puhua assisted and supported him.
Not long after the Master had taken up residence, Puhua passed away in his entirety.
Consequently, during the "Half-summer" retreat, the Master went to Huangbo and saw the Abbot reading a sutra; the Master said:
"I thought this was a man of substance; it turns out he is just an old monk who hides his black beans.
After staying for several days, [the visitor] took his leave.
Huangbo said:
"You have broken the summer retreat; did you not complete it before departing?
The Master said, "I came for a short time to pay my respects to the Honored One."
Huangbo then struck him and drove him away.
After traveling several li, the Master felt doubt regarding this matter and returned to stay for the remainder of the summer retreat.
One day, as the Master was taking his leave of Huangbo, Huangbo asked:
"Where have you gone?
The Master said, "Not south of the River; I have returned to north of the River."

Huangbo then struck him; the Master restrained him and gave him a slap with his palm. Huangbo laughed heartily and called for an attendant, saying, "Bring the meditation board and desk of our late master Baizhang."
The Master said,
"Attendant, bring some fire.
Huangbo said:
"Even so, you may take it with you; later on, you shall sit upon the tongues of all people under heaven.
Later, Guishan asked Yangshan, "Did Linji fail Huangbo?"
Yangshan said, "Not so. Guishan said:
"What about you, my son?
Yangshan replied,
"Only by knowing gratitude does one understand how to repay it."
Taisu said, "Among the ancients of old, was there anyone who was similar to this?
Yangshan replied:
“There was one, but because the era is so remote, I do not wish to cite him for you, Master.
Guishan said, “Even so, I still wish to know; you simply go ahead and cite him.”
Yangshan said: "It is just as Ānanda praised the Buddha at the assembly of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, saying:
'To offer this profound mind to the dust-motes of all lands—this is what is called repaying the Buddha's kindness.'"
"Is this not, indeed, an act of repaying kindness?
Guishan said, "So it is, so it is."
"If one's insight is equal to that of the teacher, they fall short of the teacher by half their virtue;
only when one's insight surpasses that of the teacher is one fit to receive the transmission.
The Master went to the head of Bodhidharma’s stupa, where the caretaker said:
"Venerable sir, shall I first pay homage to the Buddha,
or shall I first pay homage to the Patriarch?
The Master said:
“I do not pay homage to either the Buddha or the Patriarchs.
The stupa master asked,
“What kind of enemies are the Buddha and the Patriarchs to you, Elder?”
The Master then shook out his sleeves and departed.
While traveling on pilgrimage, the Master arrived at Longgang. When Longgang ascended the hall, the Master stepped forward and asked:
"Without deploying any sharp weapons, how can one achieve victory?"
Guang took his seat.
The Master said,
"A great spiritual friend (mahā-kalyāṇamitra), surely you have some skillful means?"
Guang stared with wide eyes and said,
"Ha! The Master pointed his finger and said:
"This old fellow has met with defeat today.
Upon arriving at Sanfeng, Master Ping asked,
"Where have you come from?"
The Master said,
"Huangbo has come. Ping said:
"What words did Huangbo have?
The Master said:
"Last night, the Golden Ox met with calamity; even until now, no trace of him is seen."
Ping said, "The golden wind blows through the jade flute; who among them is a connoisseur?
The Master said:
"Directly penetrating ten thousand layers of barriers, one does not dwell within the clear void.
Ping said, "Your question is far too lofty."
The Master said:
"A dragon gives birth to a golden phoenix chick, which pierces through the azure lapis lazuli.
Ping said:
"Please sit and have some tea," he said.
He asked again,
"Where have you recently departed from?"
The Master said,
"Longguang. Ping said:
"How has Longguang been lately?
The Master then went out.
Upon arriving at Daci, Daci was sitting within the abbot’s quarters.
The Master asked:
"When you are sitting upright in the hall, how is it?
Ciyun replied:
“The cold pines share one hue through a thousand years; the wild elder plucks a flower for spring across ten thousand lands.
The Master said:
“Ancient and modern, forever transcendent is the essence of perfect wisdom; the three mountains lock away ten thousand layers of barriers.”
Cizhen gave a shout, and the Master also shouted.
Cizhen said, "What is this?"
The Master shook out his sleeves and departed.
Upon arriving at Huayan in Xiangzhou, Huayan leaned on his staff and made the gesture of being sleepy.
The Master said, "Old monk, why are you dozing off?"
Yan said, "A master and a Zen guest are decidedly not the same.
The Master said:
"The attendant has brought tea for the Master to drink.
Yanguan then called for the Rector:
"Arrange for this senior monk to take the third seat."
Upon arriving at Cui峰 (Cui Peak), the Master of the Peak asked,
"Where have you come from?
The Master replied:
"Yellow Plum has come," said Feng. He asked,
"What words or phrases did Yellow Plum have to instruct people?"
The Master said,
"Huangbo has no words or phrases. Feng said:
"Why is it non-existent?
The Master said:
"Even if it were present, there would be no place to point it out."
Feng said, "Just bring it up and show me.
The Master said:
"A single arrow passes beyond the Western Heaven.
Upon arriving at Xiangtian, the Master asked:
"Neither ordinary nor holy—please, Master, speak quickly."
Tian said, "Does the old monk only act this way?
The Master then gave a shout and said:
"What bowl are you baldies looking for here?
When they reached Minghua, Hua asked,
"What are you doing coming and going?"
The Master said,
"You have merely worn out your straw sandals.
Huizhao said:
"Ultimately, how is it?
The Master said,
"I do not even recognize the old fellow's 'head-word' (hua-tou)."
He went toward Fenglin and encountered an old woman on the road.
The woman asked,
"Where are you going?"
The Master said,
"Fenglin departs.
The nun said:
"By chance, Fenglin was not present.
The Master asked,
"Where has he gone?"
As Ba was about to leave, the Master called out to him; Ba turned his head, and the Master struck him.
Upon arriving at Fenglin, Fenglin asked:
"Is it permissible for me to ask you a question?"
The Master said,
"How can you gouge out flesh to create a wound? Lin said:
"The sea moon is clear and without shadow; the wandering fish alone is deluded.
The Master said, "Since the sea moon has no shadow, how can the wandering fish be deluded?"
Fenglin said:
"Observing the wind, one knows the waves arise; gazing at the water, the wild sail drifts.
The Master said:
"A solitary wheel shines alone as the rivers and mountains fall silent; one self-laughing cry startles heaven and earth.
Lin said: "Let your three-inch tongue illuminate heaven and earth; try to utter a single phrase on the spot."
The Master said:
"When you encounter a swordsman on the road, you must present your sword; unless you are a poet, do not offer your poem.
Fenglin then desisted.
The Master then offered this verse:
"The Great Way transcends all sameness; let it go as it will toward the west or east. The spark from a flintstone cannot catch up;
a flash of lightning cannot penetrate. Miaoyan asked Yangshan:
"Stone-fire cannot reach it, and lightning-flash cannot penetrate it; how did the various sages of antiquity define 'a person'?
Yangshan said, "What is your intention, Master?"
Taisu said, "As long as there are words and explanations, there is no real meaning.
Yangshan said:
"Not so," said Guishan. "And how about you?"
Yangshan said, "In official matters, even a needle is not permitted; in private affairs, carriages and horses pass through.
When he arrived at Niu-tou, Niu saw the Master coming, gripped his staff crosswise, and sat crouching right at the gate.
The Master struck the staff three times with his hand and returned to sit in the first seat in the hall.
When Niu came down and saw him, he asked, "When masters and guests meet, each maintains their proper decorum; from where have you come, Venerable Elder?"
"You are being most impolite,
Master. The teacher said,
"What did the Old Monk say?"
As the ox was about to open its mouth, the Master struck it.
When the ox made a gesture as if falling over, the Master struck it again.
The ox said:
"Today was not a lucky day," said Yangshan.
Guishan then asked him,
"Between these two venerable masters, is there any victory or defeat?"
Yangshan said, "If one wins, one wins entirely; if one loses, one loses entirely.
When the Master was about to pass away, he sat upright and said:
“After my extinction, you must not allow my treasury of the true Dharma eye to perish.
The Three Sages stepped forward and said,
“How would we dare let the Master’s treasury of the true Dharma eye perish?”
The Master said,
"If someone asks you about this in the future, what will you say to him?
Sansheng then gave a shout.
The Master said,
"Who would have known that my Treasury of the True Dharma Eye would be extinguished by this blind donkey?
Having spoken these words, he passed away with a dignified and upright countenance.

The Master’s name was Yixuan; he was a native of Nanhua in Caizhou, with the secular surname Xing. From childhood he was exceptionally gifted, and as he grew up, he became renowned for his filial piety.
Upon shaving his head and receiving full ordination, he resided in lecture halls where he thoroughly investigated the Vinaya and extensively studied the sutras and śāstras.
After a while, he sighed and said: "This is merely a medical prescription for saving the world; it is not the essential meaning of that which is transmitted outside the teachings."

He then changed his robes and traveled to various regions, first visiting Huangbo and subsequently paying homage to Dayu; the dialogues and exchanges regarding these encounters are recorded in his *Xinglu* (Record of Conduct).

Having received the seal of approval from Huangbo, he soon arrived at the southeastern corner of the city of Zhenzhou in Hebei, where he resided as the abbot of a small monastery by the banks of the Hutuo River; it was for this reason that he became known as Linji.
At that time, Puhua was already there, feigning madness and mingling with the crowd, such that neither sages nor commoners could fathom him.
When the Master arrived, he immediately assisted him.
As the Master’s influence flourished, Puhua completely cast off his physical form, thereby fulfilling the prophetic prediction of Yangshan as the "Little Śākyamuni."

Coinciding with the outbreak of war, the master immediately abandoned the place and departed. Grand Marshal Mo Junhe converted his residence within the city into a temple, naming it Linji after the master’s former title, and invited the master to reside there.
Later, he brushed off his robes and traveled south to Hezhou, where the Governor, Wang the Attendant, received him with the etiquette due to a teacher.
After staying there for only a short time, he came to Xinghua Temple in Damingfu and resided in the Eastern Hall.

The Master was free from illness; suddenly one day, he adjusted his robes and sat upright. After concluding a dialogue with Sansheng, he passed away in silence. This occurred on the tenth day of the first lunar month in the eighth year of the Xiantong era of the Tang dynasty, the Dinghai year.

The disciples erected a stupa for the Master’s entire remains at the northwest corner of Daming Prefecture; by imperial decree, he was posthumously titled Chan Master Huizhao, and his stupa was named Chengling.
With palms joined and heads bowed, I record the Master’s principal deeds.
Written respectfully by his Dharma heir and junior disciple Yanzhao, residing at Baoshou Monastery in Zhenzhou.
